intro.text: You are generating a Describe Image task with a chart (graph, bar chart, line chart, pie chart, or table) for the PTE exam. The student must describe the data visually shown in the chart.

blocks.text: Generate numerical data that will be rendered into a chart, along with key points that describe important features of that data.

items: Topic: A brief title for the chart (5-10 words, no special characters)
Chart type (chartType): BAR, LINE, PIE or TABLE
Title: The chart title (the same as the topic or slightly expanded)
X label (xLabel): The label of the x-axis (optional for PIE and TABLE)
Y label (yLabel): The label of the y-axis (optional for PIE and TABLE)
Unit: The unit of the values, for example millions of dollars, percentage or number of visitors
Categories: The category name for each bar, line point or row
Series: Each series has a name and a list of numeric values

Key points (keyPoints): Each key point has a kind (MAX, MIN, TREND_UP, TREND_DOWN, COMPARE or TOTAL), a text description in the student's language (English or Vietnamese) and a reference to the series, category or value it refers to, used for validation

blocks.text:
1. BAR: 3–8 categories, 1–3 series, all values ≥ 0.
2. LINE: 3–8 categories, 1–3 series, all values ≥ 0.
3. PIE: 3–8 slices, exactly 1 series, all values ≥ 0, sum must equal 100 ± 0.5.
4. TABLE: 3–6 rows, 2–5 columns, all values ≥ 0.

1. Realistic data: use plausible numbers for the topic.
2. Mix of key point types: include MAX, MIN, TREND, and/or COMPARE.
3. 2–4 key points that highlight important insights.
4. No acronyms in title or labels.
5. Numbers as digits in the data array (not spelled out).
6. Key point text can be in English or Vietnamese; it is stored as the reference for grading.

DIFFICULTY BY CEFR LEVEL: the target level is set by the person and must be met through the data itself, staying within the chart type rules.
1. B1: one clear trend or one obvious leader; 3–5 categories; 1–2 series; whole, well-spaced values.
2. B2: 2–3 series with a clear contrast; 4–6 categories; one exception to the main pattern.
3. C1: 2–3 series whose trends differ (one rises while another falls or stays flat); 5–8 categories; at least one crossing or turning point; some values close enough to need careful comparison.
4. C2: 3 series across 6–8 categories with non-uniform patterns (rise, fall, dip then recovery); lines or bars that cross; small gaps and proportional changes that need precise, nuanced wording; data that invites synthesis (which factor dominates, what changed and when).
5. Key points grow with the level: at B1 the highest, lowest and main trend; from C1 the relationships, exceptions, turning points and reversals.
6. When a reviewer asks for more difficulty, change the data (more contrast, crossings, exceptions), not only the wording.

items: topic: Renewable Energy Adoption
chartType: BAR
title: Renewable Energy Adoption by Region (2020-2024)
xLabel: Year
yLabel: Percentage
unit: percent

keyPoints: [{"kind": "MAX", "text": "Europe had the highest renewable adoption in 2024 at fifty percent", "reference": "Europe 2024"}, {"kind": "TREND_UP", "text": "All regions showed consistent growth from 2020 to 2024", "reference": "all series"}, {"kind": "COMPARE", "text": "Europe leads both Asia and Americas by at least 18 percentage points", "reference": "Europe vs Asia"}]
Chart type is BAR, LINE, PIE, or TABLE
Number of categories within limits (3–8 for BAR/LINE, 3–8 for PIE as slices, 3–6 rows for TABLE)
All values ≥ 0
PIE: sum of series = 100 ± 0.5
Key point `kind` matches actual data (e.g., MAX must identify the actual maximum)
2–4 key points
